This is where the algorithms from Section 2.3 are put to the test. As Table 2-1 clearly demonstrates, different models excel at different tasks. The process involves training multiple candidate algorithms on the prepared data and rigorously evaluating their Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 15 performance using metrics like root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) among others. Different evaluation metrics provide different types of information and choosing which to use can depend on a multitude of factors including the need for interpretability, for balancing goodness of fit versus prediction errors, and for penalizing the size of errors. This empirical, evidence-based approach is the practical embodiment of the "No Free Lunch" theorem. The model that provides the best performance on the validation data, without showing signs of significant overfitting, is then chosen for deployment. By systematically splitting a dataset into multiple subsets, or "folds,” and repeatedly training and validating the model on different combinations of these folds, cross-validation (CV) helps provide a robust evaluation on how models perform on new or unseen data. CV helps prevent the model from memorizing specific patterns or anomalies in the training data and instead promotes the learning of generalizable patterns across diverse data samples. As a result, training a model using CV can provide a more reliable estimate of the model's real-world performance and aid in selecting models and hyperparameters that lead to robust and generalizable results. This entire workflow—from cleaning to feature selection to model training—is an iterative loop. The choice of an imputation method might affect which features are selected, which in turn influences which model performs best. Success requires a holistic view, recognizing that each step is interconnected and contributes to the final goal of building a robust, reliable, and trustworthy data-driven model. This project serves as a powerful, tangible demonstration of the NFL theorem in action. Within the confines of a single, coordinated research effort focused on the WRRF sector, no single algorithm emerged as a universal solution. The fact that a Support Vector Machine (SVM) was the top performer for carbon diversion (Application 1), XGBoost was the champion for disinfection (Application 3), P-recovery (Application 4), and biosolids optimization (Application 5), and an LSTM ensemble was essential for BNR aeration control (Application 2) provides undeniable evidence for this principle.
